performers: Pierre Mollet, baritone; women of the Chorale Élisabeth Brasseur; Orchestre des Concerts Lamoureux; Igor Markevitch, conductor
question: How does a psalm that begins “grave, rude” arrive at such a restrained close?
intro: The orchestra speaks at length before Pierre Mollet’s baritone takes up the psalm. Boulanger allowed several vocal scorings; this recording names a solo baritone, not a male chorus in his place. Follow the forceful declamation towards its unexpectedly quiet, suspended ending.

cues.title: Grave and rough
cues.text: The opening instruction is “Grave, rude.” Winds and horns carry an accented line above plucked double basses; most of the strings initially wait. Listen to the weight of that unhurried attack before the orchestra fills out.
cues.evidence: Visually inspected Durand full score, printed p. 1: https://ks15.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/7/74/IMSLP829067-PMLP430945-Boulanger,_L_-_Psalm_129_full_score.pdf. Whole-work listening point, not an assertion that a particular note or entrance occurs at this timestamp.

cues.title: An orchestra gathering weight
cues.text: The opening grows brighter and more forceful rather than remaining a static introduction. Follow the expanding sound across several phrases; the soloist has a substantial orchestral argument to answer.
cues.evidence: Actual cached mono stream: cache/analysis/lili-boulanger-psalm-129.txt, the level increases towards 0:45–1:10, with strong changes near 0:44 and 0:56 Source file: https://archive.org/details/lp_du-fond-de-labime-psaume-24-psaume-129_lili-boulanger-igor-markevitch-orchestre-d. These measurements establish the broad contour, not isolated instruments or words.

cues.title: Another Roman psalm
cues.text: Boulanger completed Psalm 129 in Rome in 1916, the same year as Psalm 24. They are separate compositions with different vocal and instrumental designs, not consecutive movements of a single choral symphony.
cues.evidence: Printed p. 25 is dated Rome 1916; composition account: https://repertoire-explorer.musikmph.de/wp-content/uploads/vorworte_prefaces/1100.html https://ks15.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/7/74/IMSLP829067-PMLP430945-Boulanger,_L_-_Psalm_129_full_score.pdf

cues.title: One voice takes the argument
cues.text: Here the vocal writing is carried by Pierre Mollet’s baritone. In the score the first vocal statement follows thirty orchestral bars, with a broad line against strongly marked accompaniment. Listen for continuity with the orchestral opening rather than a separate song beginning.
cues.evidence: Visually inspected Durand full score, printed p. 8, figure 3; the score’s prefatory performance options: https://ks15.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/7/74/IMSLP829067-PMLP430945-Boulanger,_L_-_Psalm_129_full_score.pdf. cache/analysis/lili-boulanger-psalm-129.txt: the crest near 1:30 and strong change at 1:34 provide an approximate anchor for the vocal span; the report does not detect a sung word. Approximate passage placement; no bar-to-audio alignment or exact entrance is claimed.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Triplets within the pressure
cues.text: A more flowing accompaniment changes the grain of the music: clarinets and bass clarinet move in triplets, with harp and lower lines underneath. The vocal line remains broader. Try following accompaniment and declamation as two different rates of motion.
cues.evidence: Visually inspected Durand full score, printed p. 11, figure 4: https://ks15.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/7/74/IMSLP829067-PMLP430945-Boulanger,_L_-_Psalm_129_full_score.pdf. cache/analysis/lili-boulanger-psalm-129.txt: the changes around 2:16–2:28 and reduced level in that area support an approximate middle-passage placement. Approximate passage placement; no bar-to-audio alignment or exact entrance is claimed.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Performed after her death
cues.text: The work reached the public after Boulanger’s death. The scholarly preface records its 1921 performance at the Salle Pleyel under Henri Büsser; the Everest recording issued in 1960 belongs to a later chapter in its reception.
cues.evidence: Helen Julia Minors, 2011 preface, performance history. https://repertoire-explorer.musikmph.de/wp-content/uploads/vorworte_prefaces/1100.html

cues.title: The middle still has force
cues.text: The more flowing writing has not removed the weight of the psalm. This stretch sustains a strong recorded level; listen for how a long vocal phrase can hold its shape against an active accompaniment.
cues.evidence: Actual cached mono stream: cache/analysis/lili-boulanger-psalm-129.txt, the 3:15–3:55 windows stay relatively strong, reaching approximately −4 to −6 dB in several windows Source file: https://archive.org/details/lp_du-fond-de-labime-psaume-24-psaume-129_lili-boulanger-igor-markevitch-orchestre-d. These measurements establish the broad contour, not isolated instruments or words.

cues.title: A slower destination ahead
cues.text: The score eventually turns from emphatic declamation to a slower, much quieter coda. Keep the earlier accent pattern in mind: the change will concern the manner of speaking as well as the volume.
cues.evidence: Visually inspected Durand full score, printed pp. 21–22, Cédez and figure 8; whole-work comparison: https://ks15.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/7/74/IMSLP829067-PMLP430945-Boulanger,_L_-_Psalm_129_full_score.pdf. Whole-work listening point, not an assertion that a particular note or entrance occurs at this timestamp.

cues.title: A choice in the score
cues.text: Boulanger permits a baritone soloist with optional women’s voices, a male chorus, or a mixed chorus. The Everest insert explicitly names Pierre Mollet for this track. Do not mistake the album’s general choral credit for proof that every vocal alternative is used.
cues.evidence: Per-track soloist heading; score performance options on PDF p. 3: https://ks15.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/7/74/IMSLP829067-PMLP430945-Boulanger,_L_-_Psalm_129_full_score.pdf https://i.discogs.com/YRlMh__FB1Z6EXv1xxcm1OfoUrYyEvbGNCKMou0f0aI/rs:fit/g:sm/q:90/h:600/w:599/czM6Ly9kaXNjb2dz/LWRhdGFiYXNlLWlt/YWdlcy9SLTYwNTY4/NTItMTQ3MzM1MDk5/OS01NzcxLmpwZWc.jpeg

cues.title: A different orchestral light
cues.text: The coda replaces the earlier heavy attack with long quiet lines. Women’s voices, muted strings, celesta and harp belong to this written closing texture. Listen for the accompaniment’s small motions within the sustained sound, rather than expecting a final brass proclamation.
cues.evidence: Visually inspected Durand full score, printed pp. 22–25, figure 8 onwards: https://ks15.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/7/74/IMSLP829067-PMLP430945-Boulanger,_L_-_Psalm_129_full_score.pdf. cache/analysis/lili-boulanger-psalm-129.txt: the level is much lower after roughly 4:40 and remains restrained through the ending. Approximate passage placement; no bar-to-audio alignment or exact entrance is claimed.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Words give way to sound
cues.text: The final written bars continue without words, and the harmony is not polished into an uncomplicated triumphant close. Let the last quiet resonance remain unsettled; this ending does not have to answer the opening with equal force.
cues.evidence: Visually inspected Durand full score, printed p. 25, final four bars: https://ks15.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/7/74/IMSLP829067-PMLP430945-Boulanger,_L_-_Psalm_129_full_score.pdf. cache/analysis/lili-boulanger-psalm-129.txt: the final 5:45–6:08 stretch withdraws towards the end; no exact last-word timing is claimed. Approximate passage placement; no bar-to-audio alignment or exact entrance is claimed.

transitions.title: The orchestral argument acquires a voice
transitions.how: An orchestral crescendo and broadening lead to figure 3, “a Tempo, grave et rude.” The vocal line takes up the psalm against emphatic wind chords while the strings turn into running figures. In this performance the specified baritone option puts that declamation in one voice. The new singer changes the foreground, but the orchestra’s weight and accented character connect the two spans.
transitions.evidence: Visually inspected Durand full score, printed pp. 7–8 and prefatory vocal options: https://ks15.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/7/74/IMSLP829067-PMLP430945-Boulanger,_L_-_Psalm_129_full_score.pdf. Actual cached analysis, cache/analysis/lili-boulanger-psalm-129.txt: the 1:30 crest is followed by the marked change at 1:34; this locates the passage approximately. The written mechanism is documented; its placement in this recording is approximate, not a timed word or bar alignment.

transitions.title: Triplets change the accompaniment’s grain
transitions.how: At figure 4 the clarinet family begins flowing triplets above lower sustained lines and harp. The singer’s broader declamation continues across that change of accompaniment. Boulanger avoids a wholesale break: the change of rhythmic subdivision and a lighter distribution of orchestral motion provide a new surface for the continuing argument.
transitions.evidence: Visually inspected Durand full score, printed p. 11, figure 4: https://ks15.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/7/74/IMSLP829067-PMLP430945-Boulanger,_L_-_Psalm_129_full_score.pdf. Actual cached analysis, cache/analysis/lili-boulanger-psalm-129.txt: the measured changes near 2:16 and 2:28 locate the contrasting middle region, not an exact triplet onset. The written mechanism is documented; its placement in this recording is approximate, not a timed word or bar alignment.

transitions.title: The force gives way to suspension
transitions.how: A yielding gesture leads to “Un peu plus lent” at figure 8. The score adds quiet women’s voices above the vocal line; flute, celesta and harp colour the sustained harmony, while strings are muted. Alternating bar lengths loosen the closing speech. The result is a change of texture and pace, not a triumphant brass cadence.
transitions.evidence: Visually inspected Durand full score, printed pp. 21–22, figure 8: https://ks15.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/7/74/IMSLP829067-PMLP430945-Boulanger,_L_-_Psalm_129_full_score.pdf. Actual cached analysis, cache/analysis/lili-boulanger-psalm-129.txt: levels recede through 4:35–4:45, with a change near 4:44; the coda remains substantially quieter. The written mechanism is documented; its placement in this recording is approximate, not a timed word or bar alignment.

composer.epithet: Her songs and psalms give a sustained bass, a repeated interval and the weight of a choral unison the force of a large formal argument.
facts: Daughter of Ernest and Raïssa Boulanger; younger sister of the composer, conductor and teacher Nadia Boulanger
Paris Conservatoire; composition with Paul Vidal, with extensive musical support from Nadia
First woman to win the Premier Grand Prix de Rome for musical composition, 1913
Songs, choral works, orchestral and chamber pieces; unfinished opera La Princesse Maleine
composer.background:
Lili Boulanger grew up in a Paris household where composition, singing and teaching were family work. Her father Ernest had won the Prix de Rome in 1835 and taught singing at the Conservatoire; her mother Raïssa had been his pupil. Nadia, born in 1887, was already receiving serious musical training when Lili was small. Lili learned piano and several other instruments and accompanied her sister into Conservatoire classes. Recurrent illness interrupted her education from childhood. The resulting timetable was irregular, but the musical environment was exceptionally well supplied with teachers, performers and scores.

Nadia was an early mentor and practical support; Lili’s formal composition teacher at the Conservatoire was Paul Vidal. Their training included fugue, harmony and the cantata, extending well beyond the short piano pieces through which women composers were often permitted a public identity. In 1912 illness forced Lili to withdraw from the final stage of the Prix de Rome. She returned in 1913 and won the Premier Grand Prix with Faust et Hélène, becoming the first woman to receive that composition prize. She was nineteen. Nadia had won a second prize in 1908.
